answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Collins wrote this sentence in Good to Great (2001), chapter 3, “First Who… Then What.” We confirmed the wording word for word against a scan of the 2001 HarperCollins printing, where it opens a two-sentence thought that ends “no matter where the bus goes.”

source.heading: The source: Good to Great, chapter 3

docMeta.dd: Good to Great: Why Some Companies Make the Leap… and Others Don’t
Chapter 3, “First Who… Then What”: section “First Who, Great Companies, and a Great Life” (p. 62 in the scanned 2001 printing)

source.excerpt: Adherence to the idea of “first who” might be the closest link between a great company and a great life. For no matter what we achieve, if we don’t spend the vast majority of our time with people we love and respect, we cannot possibly have a great life. But if we spend the vast majority of our time with people we love and respect—people we really enjoy being on the bus with and who will never disappoint us—then we will almost certainly have a great life, no matter where the bus goes. The people we interviewed from the good-to-great companies clearly loved what they did, largely because they loved who they did it with.
trail: The sentence appears in Collins’s Good to Great (HarperBusiness, 2001), chapter 3, in the passage that closes his discussion of “first who” (Internet Archive catalog record ↗).
Wikiquote lists the line under Good to Great, 2001, citing its quotation in Lisa Marshall’s Speak the Truth and Point to Hope (2004), p. 32 (Wikiquote: Jim Collins ↗).
Thom Rainer’s 2012 roundup of Collins quotations reproduces the full three-sentence passage (Church Answers, archived ↗).

Collins makes the same point in his own words on his website: if our time is not spent with people we love and respect, it hardly matters where the bus is going (“First Who” Is Not Just a Business Concept ↗).
source.excerptNote: The popular quote is the first sentence of this passage, copied word for word. The “bus” is the book’s running image for a company’s team: get the right people on the bus before deciding where to drive it.

author.metaLine: b. 1958 · American business researcher, author & speaker
author.bio: James C. “Jim” Collins was born in Aurora, Colorado, in 1958. He studied at Stanford and began his research and teaching career on the faculty of Stanford’s Graduate School of Business in 1988. He is best known for research-based management books, above all Good to Great (2001), which brought phrases like “Level 5 leadership” and “getting the right people on the bus” into everyday business talk.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Good to Great argued that the companies that moved from good results to great ones first chose the right people (“who”) and only then chose a direction (“what”). Collins closes chapter 3 by turning that business finding into advice about life: who you spend your days with matters more than where you are headed.

Collins has kept making this point outside the book. On his website he says “First Who, Then What” applies to life as well as business, and he describes changing his rock climbing: he stopped picking the climb first and started picking the people he would climb with (jimcollins.com ↗).
